newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dlr hits 4-year high, stocks sink on bank worries.
newsitem.headline: Dlr hits 4-year high, stocks sink on bank worries.

text.p: The dollar climbed to a four-year high against the yen on Wednesday, while Tokyo stocks slipped on renewed worries about the health of Japanese banks.

A perception that the Group of Seven (G7) industrialised nations will not come up with any concrete measures for currencies other than calling for stability of the markets at this weekend's meeting led to the heavy dollar purchases.
The dollar surged to 123 yen in afternoon trade, the highest level in 48 months. The greenback ended at around 122.47 yen in New York on Tuesday.

Meanwhile, the Tokyo stock market's Nikkei average of 225 leading shares tumbled more than two percent at one stage in the morning before recovering slightly to stand down 205.03 points or 1.12 percent at 18,109.30 by midday.
A weak Japanese stock market hurts the yen as it reduces the attraction of investing in assets in Japan, helping the dollar.
"The G7 meeting may end up with only a call for stability in currency rates, which means that a gradual dollar rise would be possible beyond the meeting," said a dealer at a major Japanese bank.
Finance ministers and central bank governors of the United States, Japan, Germany, France, Britain, Italy and Canada will meet in Berlin on Saturday.
Worries over the outlook for Japan's economy, brought on by doubts over the health of the country's financial institutions, also fuelled sales of yen for dollars.
Rumours about Nippon Credit Bank Ltd's financial health reignited worries over Japan's banking sector and spurred a round of dollar buying on Wednesday, dealers said.

Japanese government bond prices also reacted strongly to market talk that the bank would hold an emergency news conference as early as today, but the bank later denied the rumours. The key March bond futures contract rose as high as 126.65 by midday, up sharply from the previous day's 126.22.

Although Nippon Credit said that it saw no cause for concern about its own financial health, worries about the health of some Japanese banks could persist ahead of the end of the fiscal year in March.
"This kind of market rumour has tended to serve in favour of yen sales," said a currency dealer.
"There was a variety of rumours about the bank (Nippon Credit), and they fanned market fears," said Michio Sugita, head of stock trading at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
News of a rise in Japan's trade deficit for the first 20 days of January had lifted the dollar against the yen in the morning.

Japan's customs-cleared trade deficit rose 23.4 percent to 350.68 billion yen ($2.87 billion) in the first 20 days of January compared with a revised deficit of 284.28 billion yen ($2.33 billion) in the same period a year earlier.

Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said in the afternoon that an excessively weak or strong yen was undesirable and added that stable foreign exchange rates were important for Japan's economy. Those comments had little effect on the forex market as they were basically a rehash of what he said earlier.
